mcqs.q: The PRIMARY function of cementum is:
opts: Attachment of the collagen fibres that bind the tooth to alveolar bone
mcqs.explain: The primary function of cementum is anchorage — attachment of the collagen (Sharpey's) fibres binding the tooth to the alveolar bone.

mcqs.q: Hypophosphatasia, with almost total absence of cementum, characteristically causes:
opts: Loosening and premature loss of anterior deciduous teeth
mcqs.explain: Hypophosphatasia (an inherited disease with near-total absence of cementum) causes loosening and premature loss of the anterior deciduous teeth.

mcqs.q: Cementum contributes to functional ADAPTATION by:
opts: Apical deposition that compensates for occlusal (incisal) wear
mcqs.explain: Deposition of cementum in the apical area compensates for loss of tooth substance from occlusal wear; cementum is normally not resorbed.

mcqs.q: The cementum formed during REPAIR is usually:
mcqs.explain: Repair cementum is usually cellular because it forms faster; if repair is slow it may resemble primary (acellular) cementum.

mcqs.q: Cementum receives its nutrition from:
opts: The surrounding vascular periodontal ligament (it is avascular)
mcqs.explain: Cementum is avascular and lacks a nerve supply; it is nourished by the surrounding vascular periodontal ligament.

mcqs.q: Continuous formation of cementum helps to:
opts: Maintain the width of the periodontal ligament
mcqs.explain: Continuous deposition of cementum maintains the width of the periodontal ligament throughout the life of the tooth.

mcqs.q: With age, cementum thickness:
opts: Increases, especially at the apex (roughly triples from age 10 to 75)
mcqs.explain: Cementum thickness increases with age, particularly at the apex due to active eruption, tripling from about age 10 to 75.

mcqs.q: As cementum thickens with age, the deep cementocytes:
opts: Gradually die (reduced access to nutrition and waste removal)
mcqs.explain: As the width increases, deeper cementocytes lose access to nutrition and waste elimination and gradually die.

mcqs.q: Hypercementosis classically appears as:
opts: Nodular thickening of the apical third of the root
mcqs.explain: Hypercementosis is an abnormal thickening of cementum, classically a nodular enlargement of the apical third of the root.

mcqs.q: GENERALIZED hypercementosis is associated with:
mcqs.explain: Generalized hypercementosis is associated with Paget's disease; localized forms occur with cementoblastoma, acromegaly, arthritis, etc.

mcqs.q: Localized spur/prong-like hypercementosis typically develops in teeth subjected to:
opts: Great occlusal stress (more surface area gives firmer anchorage)
mcqs.explain: Spur/prong-like hypercementosis forms in teeth under great stress, giving a larger surface area for fibre attachment and firmer anchorage.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, an area of hypercementosis is:
opts: Enveloped by the PDL shadow and lamina dura, as in normal cementum
mcqs.explain: Radiographically, the radiolucent PDL shadow and the radiopaque lamina dura always envelope the hypercementosis, as around normal cementum.

mcqs.q: Compared with bone, cementum is:
opts: More resistant to resorption (because it is avascular)
mcqs.explain: Cementum is more resistant to resorption than bone because it is avascular; resorption follows trauma or excessive occlusal forces.

mcqs.q: In ANATOMIC repair of resorbed cementum:
opts: The original outline of the root surface is re-established
Only a thin layer forms and the outline is not restored
mcqs.explain: Anatomic repair re-establishes the root surface outline; functional repair lays only a thin layer and restores PDL width via a bony projection.

mcqs.q: FUNCTIONAL repair of cementum resorption restores the PDL width by:
opts: Complete re-formation of the root outline
mcqs.explain: In functional repair, only a thin cementum layer forms; the normal PDL width is restored by formation of a bony projection.

mcqs.q: Fragments of cementum severed from the dentin after a severe blow are called:
mcqs.explain: A severe blow can cause cemental tears — fragments of cementum severed from the underlying dentin.

mcqs.q: Fusion of bone and cementum produces:
mcqs.explain: Abnormal cemental deposition can fuse bone and cementum, causing ankylosis (loss of the PDL space).

mcqs.q: The inorganic content of cementum (45%) compared with bone (67%) means cementum is:
mcqs.explain: Cementum is ~45% inorganic / 55% organic + water, whereas bone is ~67% inorganic / 33% organic — so cementum is less mineralized.

mcqs.q: The rate of apposition of acellular cementum versus lamellar bone is:
mcqs.explain: Acellular cementum is deposited at 0.005–0.01 µm/day, far slower than lamellar bone at 1–2 µm/day.

mcqs.q: Which feature is shared by BOTH cementum and bone?
opts: Hydroxyapatite mineral and type I collagen
mcqs.explain: Both contain hydroxyapatite, type I collagen, and non-collagenous proteins (BSP, osteopontin); cementum, however, is avascular, non-innervated and remodels poorly.

mcqs.q: Cemental caries occurs:
mcqs.explain: Cemental caries develops on exposed cementum (root) surfaces, e.g. after gingival recession.

mcqs.q: Plaque and its by-products in periodontal pockets:
opts: Alter the physical, chemical and structural properties of cementum (interfering with healing)
mcqs.explain: In periodontal pockets, plaque alters cementum's properties; these altered surfaces must be removed mechanically/chemically for healing.

saqs.q: List the three functions of cementum.
saqs.a: Anchorage (attaches PDL fibres to bone — primary), adaptation (apical deposition compensates for occlusal wear), and repair (of fractures/resorptions, usually by cellular cementum).

saqs.q: Why is cementum avascular significant clinically?
saqs.a: It is nourished by the surrounding PDL, has no nerve supply, and is more resistant to resorption than bone; continuous formation maintains the PDL width.

saqs.q: Describe the age changes of cementum.
saqs.a: Thickness increases with age, especially at the apex (active eruption), tripling from age 10 to 75; deeper cementocytes die from poor nutrition.

saqs.q: Define hypercementosis and give two associations.
saqs.a: Abnormal thickening of cementum (nodular apical-third enlargement). Associations: Paget's disease (generalized), heavy occlusal stress, cementoblastoma, acromegaly, arthritis.

saqs.q: Contrast anatomic and functional repair of cementum resorption.
saqs.a: Anatomic: the root outline is re-established. Functional: only a thin cementum layer forms and the PDL width is restored by a bony projection.

saqs.q: Give three differences between cementum and bone.
saqs.a: Cementum: 45% mineral (vs 67%), avascular & non-innervated (vs vascular/innervated), slow apposition & limited remodelling (vs fast/effective), more resorption-resistant.

saqs.q: Name two clinical conditions of cementum besides hypercementosis.
saqs.a: Cemental tears (after a severe blow), ankylosis (bone–cementum fusion), and cemental caries on exposed roots.
